speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Indeed, the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) monitors closely the development of these drone incidents, so that we can assess the adequacy of our defence systems and to plug gaps when identified.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Over the past decade, SAF has enhanced our air defence systems against possible drone attacks.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The recent Saudi attack reflects the growing and evolving capabilities of drones that are available to both state and non-state actors who mean to do us harm.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: While reports still need to be confirmed, that attack shows clearly that the range and manoeuvrability of drones have increased, depending on the reports you read, from 700 kilometres (km) to 1,500 km.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These medium- and long-range drones are able to avoid radar detection and also hit their targets with great precision.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Many Members would have seen the pictures after the attacks and how precise those attacks were.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Saudi attack was conducted by sophisticated weaponised drones and that represents one extreme of sophistication in terms of drone capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If we take the other extreme where you have simple drones that can be bought in retail stores and that would intrude into restricted air space, but even though they are very simple devices, they can disrupt civilian or military air traffic because they pose safety hazards.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The impact is not trivial, as the past incidents in Gatwick and Changi Airport showed.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In both incidents, planes were diverted and grounded which resulted in both real and opportunity costs amounting to millions to airport regulators, airlines and passengers.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These simple off-the-shelf drones can be modified with some know-how to avoid detection by conventional means that most commercial airports employ.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, on one hand, very sophisticated, weaponised drones that can go up to 1,500 km; and the other extreme, toy drones that you can buy from the stores that create great impact.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Between these two extremes are the class of drones that can carry simple munitions, such as grenades and small arms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For example, the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) had been successful in modifying and weaponising small drones with explosives to attack ground forces and facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In August 2018, drones carrying explosives were used in an attempted attack on the President of Venezuela.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Taken as a whole, the security threats posed by drones are, therefore, real and the impact can be damaging, even devastating, depending on the platform used.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Against this wide spectrum of threats, there can be no single counter-response.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It would neither be proportionate nor sustainable to employ sophisticated assets worth hundreds of millions of dollars to take down hobbyist drones that can be bought for less than a thousand dollars.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For these threats, other tools would be required, such as regulations, deterrent fines and penalties, education and working with relevant stakeholders, including the drone-hobbyist communities themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Ministry of Transport (MOT) has been very busy doing that and we are passing some Bills to enhance penalties.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For Changi Airport, MOT and the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) deal with possible intrusions from drones.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) and the Singapore Police Force (SPF) take the lead in defending against drones in specific areas of security concern and during major events.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The SAF will assist them when called upon and when needed.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Beyond these specific responsibilities by various agencies against drones in their geographic domains, SAF remains responsible for drone attacks against Singapore by would-be aggressors, especially towards key installations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For example, SAF recognises that terrorists can use drones as a form of attack.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Within our region, an ISIS-linked individual had planned to use commercial drones to conduct bomb attacks in Malaysia.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Singapore continues to be a target for regional terrorist groups, as demonstrated by the foiled terrorist attack on Marina Bay Sands in 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These incidents are sober reminders that the risks are not theoretical and we must remain vigilant.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Republic of Singapore Air Force (RSAF) has enhanced its early warning capability with more capable sensors like the G550 Airborne Early Warning Aircraft and Multi-Mission Radars.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: After identification, these drones would be taken down by our Ground-Based Air Defence (GBAD) systems, which have now been upgraded with new platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some Members, as National Service (NS)men and Ground-based Air Defence (GBAD) units, would have been familiar with the old systems.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF is confident that these systems can protect Singapore against aerial threats from both manned and unmanned aircraft.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I also mentioned drones in the middle part of that threat spectrum.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These threats are rapidly evolving and while they may not cause large-scale damage, they can cause bodily harm, undermine confidence and disrupt our society.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Just imagine if grenades were dropped or suicide attacks with minor explosives were used.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Against such threats, as we did in the National Day Parade or during the Trump-Kim Summit held in Singapore, SAF puts up additional sensors and counter-offensive capabilities when required during high signature events or when intelligence assessments indicate specific risks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, do we have military hardware, the assets, to counter the military threat of a military-grade unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) attack or a military drone attack?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, would our air defence continue to provide a protective umbrella over Singapore, notwithstanding the advent of military-grade drones and UAVs, and the threat they pose?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second question – I agree that the solution does not depend solely on the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, how will drone hobbyists be made to abide by rules, such as to avoid air space close to key installations, which, in turn, will help our authorities quickly detect, isolate and neutralise the real and harmful threats?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, let us take the first threat that Mr Christopher de Souza mentioned about – the sophisticated drones.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There, as a whole, most militaries, including the SAF, are more confident.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because once you go beyond a certain size, whether it is manned or unmanned, your air defence systems are up.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is the other spectrums that are more troublesome, sometimes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Hobbyist drones – how do you deal with them?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is inappropriate to use the systems that we use against large weaponised drones for them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There, I would say that the industry is busily working because it is a global issue.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Many airports can be affected as we saw in Gatwick and Changi; and our own scientists and SAF are also looking for appropriate measures that are sustainable and cost-effective.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As well as against the intermediate set of spectrum that I talked about, in other words, larger sized drones, not quite as big as the ones that are used in the Saudi attack, but nonetheless can carry small arms, small ammunitions and grenades, and so on and so forth.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, you can require it and regulations will form part of our toolbox against such aspects.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the main, that will help reduce the noise.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In other words, you put in those regulations and, by and large, the majority of distributors and hobbyists will comply with the rules, and that reduces the noise so that you can focus on the errant drone operators.
